newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Federal Reserve keeps interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Federal Reserve keeps interest rates steady.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The Federal Reserve on Tuesday left interest rates unchanged at a policy meeting closely watched by world financial markets.

The decision, which had been anxiously awaited on Wall Street and at the White House, left the key federal funds rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans unchanged at 5-1/4 percent. It also left the discount rate, which the Fed charges banks, unchanged at 5 percent.
"The Federal Open Market Committee meeting ended at 1:40 p.m. (1740 GMT)," central bank spokesman Joseph Coyne said. "There is no further announcement."
The bland statement hid what analysts believed was one of the more contentious meetings of the Fed's policy-making committee.
Anti-inflation hawks at the Fed, particularly at its regional banks, have made no secret of their desire for higher rates to cool off the economy and keep inflation at bay.
Tuesday's decision was good news for President Bill Clinton, who has been counting on a trouble-free economy in the approach to the Nov. 5 election to help him win a second, four-year term.
Clinton said he thought the decision to leave interest rates unchanged showed that the economy was strong with no signs of inflation.
"I just think it shows we've got a strong economy with no inflation. I'm glad about that," Clinton said during a campaign visit to New Jersey.
Many analysts still expect the Fed to raise interest rates sometime in the coming months, possibly at its next policy meeting on Nov. 13 -- eight days after the election.
Central bank policy-makers were faced with conflicting evidence on the state of the economy when they met on Tuesday.
By opting not to raise rates now, the Fed is hoping that economic growth will slow enough on its own to head off the risk of higher inflation, analysts said.
In the words of Fed Gov. Janet Yellen, the economy is operating in an "inflationary danger zone." But so far, there is no clear sign of higher inflation.
At 5.1 percent, the unemployment rate is at its lowest point in more than seven years and at a level that in the past has often led to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation.
Wages, in fact, have already begun to pick up. But so far, companies have been unable to pass through those higher labour costs to consumers in the form of price increases.
Much will depend on the future course of the economy.

In the second quarter, the economy grew at a 4.8 percent clip -- its fastest pace in two years and about twice the rate most analysts reckon is sustainable on a long-term basis without fanning inflation.
Growth has shown signs of slowing since then. Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of economic activity, has slowed.

But with consumer confidence steady at about a six-year high, labour markets tight and wages rising, some analysts and Fed anti-inflation hawks question whether the developing slowdown will be enough to keep price pressures in check.
The central bank was under considerable political pressure not to raise rates Tuesday, six weeks ahead of the election.
Seventy-eight lawmakers -- all but two of them Democrats -- wrote to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on Monday contending that a rate rise now would hurt, not help the economy.
Clinton administration officials have argued that inflation remained quiescent, strongly implying that they saw no need for the independent central bank to raise rates.
